body.statement:
The asserted all-prefix coupling with covariance \(\Gamma_n\) is false on \(\mathcal P^{\mathrm{reg}}\) as defined.  For an admissible choice of the fixed constants there is a sequence \(\mathbf P\in\mathcal P^{\mathrm{reg}}\), an interior prefix \(k_n/n_{\mathcal E}\to1/2\), and oracle nuisance learners for which the generated ordering is, with probability tending to one, the ordinary order of a continuous score, but
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau_{n,k_n}-\tau_n-b_{n,k_n}\}
\]
has a non-Gaussian subsequential limit and hence cannot be coupled within \(o_{\mathbb P_n}(1)\) to \(G_{n,k_n}\sim N(0,\Gamma_n(k_n,k_n))\).  The missing first-order term is the empirical fixed-cardinality quantile-boundary term; estimating the ranking score may add a further boundary derivative.
body.proof_tex:
Because the assertion is existential, choose admissible fixed constants with \(q=5\), \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), and \(C\) large enough to dominate all of the bounded quantities below.  Put \(n_{\mathcal R}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), \(n_{\mathcal E}=n-n_{\mathcal R}\), and complete the finitely many initial rows in any way satisfying the same strict inequalities.  Write \(M_n=\max\{1,\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\}\) and fix numbers \(a_0>0\) and \(\sigma_0,\sigma_1>0\), all sufficiently small relative to \(C\).

We first give an anchor-exact law.  Conditional on \(R=1\), let \(X\) have density one half on each of \([-2,-1]\) and \([1,2]\), let \(A\) be an independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) variable, and let \(E_a\), \(a\in\{0,1\}\), be independent centered Rademacher variables taking values \(\pm\sigma_a\).  If \(X=1+u\), \(0\leq u\leq1\), set
\[
 \Delta_n(u)=a_0\cos(2\pi M_nu),\qquad
 Y(a)=1+u-\Delta_n(u)+E_a,
\]
and if \(X=-1-u\), set \(Y(a)=-1-u+E_a\).  Conditional on \(R=0\), let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), put \(X=1+U\), \(A=0\), and \(Y(0)=Y(1)=Y=1+U\).  Finally take \(V\) uniform and independent of all the preceding variables.  Consistency then holds by construction and trial randomization holds because \(A\) is independent of \((X,Y(0),Y(1))\).

Use the genuine squared outcome-regression loss
\[
 L((x,y);\theta)=\{y-\mu_0(x;\theta)\}^2,
 \qquad \mu_0(x;\theta)=\theta,
 \qquad \Theta=\mathbb R.
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(M_n\) is an integer, \(\int_0^1\Delta_n(u)\,du=0\).  The two covariate components have opposite means, so
\[
 E_{P_n}(Y\mid R=1,A=0)
 =\frac12\int_0^1(1+u-\Delta_n(u))\,du
  +\frac12\int_0^1(-1-u)\,du=0.
\]
Consequently the risk in (1) has the unique interior minimizer \(\theta_n=0\), its Hessian is \(H_n=2\), and the score equation in \(\mathrm{ass:score\text{-}equation}\) holds.  For an external point \(z=(1+u,1+u,v)\), the displayed definition of \(s_n\) gives
\[
 s_n(z)=2E_{P_n}(|Y|\mid R=1,A=0)(1+u).
 \tag{2}
\]
The factor in front of \(1+u\) is bounded above and away from zero: the negative covariate component alone gives a uniform positive lower bound when \(a_0,\sigma_0\) are chosen small.  Thus the conditional law of \(s_n(Z)\) given \(R=0\) has a density bounded uniformly in \(n\), which proves \(\mathrm{ass:score\text{-}margin}\).

The empirical minimizer in the frozen construction is the trial-control sample mean \(\widehat\theta_n\), and \(\widehat H_n=2\).  Conditional on a nonempty trial-control sample,
\[
 \widehat s_n(1+u,1+u,v)
 =2\left\{n_{\mathcal R,0}^{-1}
   \sum_{i\leq n_{\mathcal R}:A_i=0}|Y_i-\widehat\theta_n|\right\}
   |1+u-\widehat\theta_n|.
 \tag{3}
\]
Bounded second moments, the fixed-stratum sampling assumption, and Chebyshev's inequality give \(\widehat\theta_n=o_{\mathbb P_n}(1)\), while the probability of an empty control arm tends to zero.  On the event \(|\widehat\theta_n|<1/2\), the last factor in (3) is \(1+u-\widehat\theta_n\), a strictly increasing function of \(u\).  Hence, with probability tending to one, the generated ranks are exactly the ordinary ranks of the continuous variable \(U\); the label \(V\) is never used.

We next verify the local-bias restriction rather than assume it.  For a population prefix fraction \(v=k/n_{\mathcal E}\), let
\[
 \pi_n^+=\frac{\lambda_{n,\mathcal R}/2}
 {\lambda_{n,\mathcal R}/2+\lambda_{n,\mathcal E}},
 \qquad
 B_n=\frac{1-\pi_n^+}{1-\pi_n^+/2}.
\]
On the retained part \(0\leq u\leq v\) of the positive component, the trial conditional mean is \(1+u-\Delta_n(u)\), the external mean is \(1+u\), and direct conditioning in the definition of \(m_{n,k,0}\) yields
\[
 m_{n,k,0}(1+u)
 =1+u-\Delta_n(u)+B_n\Delta_n(u).
 \tag{4}
\]
Outside that part, \(m_{n,k,0}=m_{n,k,1}\).  Taking the conditional expectation of the displayed \(\eta_{n,k}\), both residual terms vanish by the definitions of \(m_{n,k,a}\); therefore
\[
 b_{n,k}=T_{n,k}-\tau_n
 =E_{P_n}\{m_{n,k,1}(X)-m_{n,k,0}(X)\mid R=1\}
 =-\frac{B_n}{2}\int_0^v\Delta_n(u)\,du.
 \tag{5}
\]
Here \(\tau_n=0\), because the two potential outcomes have the same conditional mean.  Since \(0\leq B_n\leq1\),
\[
 \max_{k\in\mathcal K_n}|\sqrt n\,b_{n,k}|
 \leq \frac{a_0\sqrt n}{4\pi M_n}=O(1),
 \tag{6}
\]
which is \(\mathrm{ass:local\text{-}misspecification}\) after increasing \(C\) if necessary.

All remaining class conditions can now be checked individually.  The source posterior is one on the negative trial-only component and equals
\(
(\lambda_{n,\mathcal R}/2)/(\lambda_{n,\mathcal R}/2+\lambda_{n,\mathcal E})
\)
on the common positive component, so \(\mathrm{ass:source\text{-}overlap}\) holds for the chosen \(\varepsilon\); treatment overlap is exactly one half.  Outcomes and scores are uniformly bounded, proving the outcome and score moment conditions.  The loss (1) is convex and twice continuously differentiable, its Hessian is the constant two, and both equicontinuity conditions are identities.  The independent uniform construction of \(V\) proves the two tie assumptions.  For nuisance estimation choose the oracle functions themselves on every fold, so every nuisance error is zero; with \(r_n=(n+1)^{-1/3}\),
\[
 \sqrt n\,r_n^2\log(en)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus the constructed sequence belongs to \(\mathcal P^{\mathrm{reg}}\).  This is an assumption-by-assumption inclusion bridge, and (1)--(3) show that it uses exactly a squared outcome-regression empirical risk minimizer and its empirical influence score, rather than a generic convex loss unrelated to the outcome.

It remains to prove the asserted non-Gaussian boundary law.  Restrict to the subsequence \(n=(2m)^2\).  Then \(n_{\mathcal R}=n_{\mathcal E}=n/2\), set \(k_n=n_{\mathcal E}/2\), and put \(p=p_{n,k_n}=3/4\).  At the population threshold \(u=1/2\),
\[
 q_{n,k_n}=\frac23,\qquad
 \pi_{n,k_n}(1+u)=\frac13,\qquad
 e_{n,k_n}(1+u)=\frac16
 \quad (u<1/2).
\]
Equation (4) specializes to
\[
 m_{n,k_n,0}(1+u)
 =1+u-\frac15\Delta_n(u),
 \qquad m_{n,k_n,1}(1+u)=1+u-\Delta_n(u).
\]
Substitution into the frozen estimating function gives, at an external record,
\[
 \eta_{n,k_n}(O)=-\frac3{25}\Delta_n(u)quad(u<1/2),
 \qquad
 \eta_{n,k_n}(O)=-3\Delta_n(u)quad(u>1/2).
 \tag{7}
\]
The second equality uses the trial-only nuisance values \(\pi=1\), \(e=1/2\), and \(m_0=m_1=1+u-\Delta_n(u)\) beyond the population threshold.  Also (5) and \(M_n=2m\) give \(b_{n,k_n}=T_{n,k_n}=0\).

Let \(\widetilde\tau_{n,k_n}\) be the same oracle estimator with the external weight replaced by \(\mathbf1\{U_j\leq1/2\}\), let \(\widehat q_n=U_{(k_n)}\), and write
\[
 N_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathcal E}}\mathbf1\{U_j\leq1/2\},
 \qquad X_n=\sqrt n(\widehat q_n-1/2).
\]
By (3), the generated prefix is \(U_j\leq\widehat q_n\) with probability tending to one.  Hence (7) gives
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{n,k_n}-\widetilde\tau_{n,k_n})
 =\frac1{p\sqrt n}
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle \frac{3a_0}{25}
   \sum_{\widehat q_n<U_j\leq1/2}\cos(2\pi\sqrt n,U_j),&N_n>k_n,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle -3a_0
   \sum_{1/2<U_j\leq\widehat q_n}\cos(2\pi\sqrt n,U_j),&N_n<k_n.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{8}
\]

For completeness, both limit steps used on the random boundary are derived here.  Expanding the characteristic function of the centered Bernoulli count at order two shows
\[
 \frac{N_n-n_{\mathcal E}/2}{\sqrt n}\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,1/8).
 \tag{9}
\]
For every fixed \(B\), the centered number of observations in an interval of length at most \(2B/\sqrt n\) has variance \(O(\sqrt n)\).  Exponential Markov's inequality applied to the bounded Bernoulli summands gives, uniformly over a grid of mesh \(n^{-1}\) in that interval, a tail bounded by \(2\exp(-c\sqrt n)\) for deviations exceeding a fixed multiple of \(\sqrt n\).  A union bound over \(O(n)\) grid intervals and monotonicity between grid points therefore yield
\[
 \sup_{|x|\leq B}\left|
 \sqrt n\{F_{n,\mathcal E}(1/2+x/\sqrt n)-F_{n,\mathcal E}(1/2)-x/\sqrt n\}
 \right|=o_{\mathbb P_n}(1).
 \tag{10}
\]
The order-statistic identity \(F_{n,\mathcal E}(\widehat q_n)=1/2\), up to an error at most \(n_{\mathcal E}^{-1}\), together with (9)--(10), proves
\[
 X_n=-2\frac{N_n-n_{\mathcal E}/2}{\sqrt n}+o_{\mathbb P_n}(1)
 \ \Rightarrow\ X,\qquad X\sim N(0,1/2).
 \tag{11}
\]
The same grid argument, now applied to the bounded variables
\(
\cos(2\pi\sqrt n,U_j)\mathbf1\{U_j\in I\}
\),
shows uniformly over these \(O(n^{-1/2})\)-length boundary intervals that the centered sum divided by \(\sqrt n\) is \(o_{\mathbb P_n}(1)\).  Thus each sum in (8) may be replaced by its expectation.  For fixed \(x\), the fact that \(\sqrt n=2m\) gives exactly
\[
 \sqrt n\int_{1/2}^{1/2+x/\sqrt n}
 \cos(2\pi\sqrt n,u)\,du
 =\frac{\sin(2\pi x)}{2\pi}.
 \tag{12}
\]
Combining (8), (11), and (12), with \(\lambda_{n,\mathcal E}=1/2\), proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{n,k_n}-\widetilde\tau_{n,k_n})
 \Rightarrow
 H(X):=-\frac{3a_0\lambda_{\mathcal E}}{2\pi p}
 \left\{\mathbf1(X>0)+\frac1{25}\mathbf1(X<0)\right\}\sin(2\pi X).
 \tag{13}
\]

The fixed-threshold statistic satisfies
\[
 \sqrt n(\widetilde\tau_{n,k_n}-T_{n,k_n})
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n
 \left[\psi_{n,k_n}(O_i)-E\{\psi_{n,k_n}(O_i)\mid R_i\}\right].
 \tag{14}
\]
For every linear combination of (14) and the centered count in (9), each summand is bounded and of order \(n^{-1/2}\).  Taylor expansion of its characteristic function has total third-order remainder \(O(n^{-1/2})\), so multiplication over the independent fixed strata proves a bivariate Gaussian limit.  Its covariance matrices converge by direct integration of \(1\), \(\cos(2\pi\sqrt n\,u)\), and \(\cos^2(2\pi\sqrt n\,u)\).  Moreover, the covariance between (14) and the count is exactly zero on this subsequence, because its only external contribution is proportional to
\[
 \int_0^{1/2}\cos(2\pi\sqrt n\,u)\,du=0.
\]
Therefore (14) converges to a centered Gaussian variable \(Z\sim N(0,v)\), \(\Gamma_n(k_n,k_n)\to v\), and \(Z\) is independent of \(X\).

Equations (13)--(14) now give
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau_{n,k_n}-\tau_n-b_{n,k_n}\}
 \Rightarrow Z+H(X).
 \tag{15}
\]
The variable \(H(X)\) is bounded and nonconstant.  If the right-hand side of (15) were Gaussian, independence would imply that the characteristic function of \(H(X)\) is the quotient of two Gaussian characteristic functions.  If the quotient has negative quadratic exponent it has modulus greater than one; if its quadratic exponent is zero it is the characteristic function of a constant; and if it is positive it is the characteristic function of a nondegenerate Gaussian.  All three alternatives contradict bounded nonconstancy.  Hence (15) is non-Gaussian.  Since \(G_{n,k_n}\Rightarrow N(0,v)\), an \(o_{\mathbb P_n}(1)\) coupling to \(G_{n,k_n}\) would force the Gaussian limit by Slutsky's identity, contradicting (15).  This proves the theorem and identifies the omitted term as the empirical fixed-cardinality quantile-boundary term.
body.justification: The counterexample now uses exactly the anchor's squared outcome-regression empirical risk minimizer and generated influence score; the score is continuous and its empirical ordering is preserved with probability tending to one.
body.gap: The fixed-set Gaussian expansion omits the empirical fixed-cardinality quantile boundary when promoted to the generated all-prefix path.
body.consumer: It rules out calibration based on the frozen covariance process, while making no claim about which coordinate the MSE selector chooses.
